questions.prompt: Why does the Church call it fitting -- not merely possible, but actually fitting -- that God himself became man, rather than saving humanity some other way?
choices: Only a divine Person, acting in a real human nature, could offer a sacrifice of infinite worth from within
Because God had no other real options available to him at all
Because becoming man was the easiest possible option for God
Because the Incarnation was simply an accident of history, with no real theological reasoning behind it
questions.correctAnswer: Only a divine Person, acting in a real human nature, could offer a sacrifice of infinite worth from within
questions.explanation: The Incarnation is not presented as the only conceivable way God could have acted, but as a truly fitting one: only God himself, acting through a real human nature, could offer a sacrifice of truly infinite worth while still genuinely standing in humanity's own place.
questions.hint: Consider what a merely human savior, or a purely divine act with no real human nature involved, would each still be missing.

citations.quote: The Church calls 'Incarnation' the fact that the Son of God assumed a human nature in order to accomplish our salvation in it.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Incarnation means the Son of God assumed a real human nature specifically in order to accomplish our salvation in it.
questions.explanation: True. The Incarnation was not simply God appearing in human form -- the Son of God took on a genuine human nature, precisely so that salvation could be accomplished within that real, assumed humanity.
questions.hint: Recall what the previous level's own real teaching already established about the Incarnation's real purpose.

citations.quote: The Church calls 'Incarnation' the fact that the Son of God assumed a human nature in order to accomplish our salvation in it.

questions.prompt: A famous patristic line, echoed at CCC 460, states the Incarnation's own real purpose in a single, striking sentence. What does it say?
choices: "The Son of God became man so that we might become God"
"The Son of God became man so that we might become angels"
"The Son of God became man so that the world might end sooner"
"The Son of God became man so that his own divinity might be reduced"
questions.correctAnswer: "The Son of God became man so that we might become God"
questions.explanation: This startling line -- meaning real participation in God's own divine life, called divinization, never a literal equality with God -- names the Incarnation's own deepest real purpose: not only forgiveness, but a real share in God's own life.
questions.hint: This is the same real line this topic's own later capstone level will return to directly.

citations.quote: For the Son of God became man so that we might become God.

questions.prompt: True or False: 'The Son of God became man so that we might become God' means a Christian literally becomes equal to God in nature.
questions.explanation: False, and this real, careful distinction matters -- this line describes divinization, a real participation in God's own divine life through grace, never a literal equality of nature. The real distinction between Creator and creature is never erased.
questions.hint: Consider whether 'a real share in God's life' and 'literal equality with God' actually mean the same thing.

citations.quote: For the Son of God became man so that we might become God.

questions.prompt: Why couldn't a merely human savior -- however holy -- have accomplished what Christ actually accomplished?
choices: A merely human offering, however holy, would still be finite -- the real debt required infinite worth
Because God specifically forbade any human being from ever trying to be holy
Because humanity's real problem was never actually serious enough to need any real solution at all
Because a human savior would have been just as effective as a divine one, with no real difference
questions.correctAnswer: A merely human offering, however holy, would still be finite -- the real debt required infinite worth
questions.explanation: This is the real crux of why the Incarnation is fitting rather than one option among equals -- only a divine Person, acting through a real human nature, could offer something of genuinely infinite worth on humanity's own behalf.
questions.hint: Consider the real difference between a finite offering and an infinite one, given the real weight of what needed to be repaired.

citations.quote: The Church calls 'Incarnation' the fact that the Son of God assumed a human nature in order to accomplish our salvation in it.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Incarnation answers both the problem this topic named several levels back (the Fall) and the real longing this topic named just one level back (the human heart's own desire for God).
questions.explanation: True, and naming this real connection directly is exactly this level's own point -- the Incarnation is not a separate, unrelated doctrine, but the Church's own real answer to both the wound this topic traced at level 3 and the real longing it traced at level 5.
questions.hint: Recall both the Fall, several levels back, and the human heart's own desire for God, one level back.

citations.quote: For the Son of God became man so that we might become God.

questions.prompt: What real word does theology use for the claim that the Incarnation, while not strictly the only conceivable way, was nonetheless the real, most appropriate way for God to save humanity?
choices: Fittingness
Necessity
Accident
Impossibility
questions.explanation: Theologians distinguish strict logical necessity (God had no other option) from fittingness (this was the real, most appropriate way, given who God is and what humanity actually needed) -- the Church holds the Incarnation was fitting, not that God could not have acted otherwise.
questions.hint: This is the exact word this level's own opening question already used to frame the whole discussion.

citations.quote: The Church calls 'Incarnation' the fact that the Son of God assumed a human nature in order to accomplish our salvation in it.

questions.prompt: Match each fact about the Incarnation's own real fittingness to what it actually means.

pairs.right: Divinization -- real participation in God's own life through grace, never a literal equality of nature
Only a divine Person could offer a sacrifice equal to humanity's real debt
The offering had to be made genuinely from within humanity, not only on its behalf from outside
The most truly appropriate way, given who God is, not the only conceivable option

questions.explanation: These four facts together explain why the Church calls the Incarnation fitting rather than arbitrary -- a real, reasoned answer to both humanity's real debt and its real, deepest longing.
questions.hint: Two rows describe what the Incarnation actually accomplishes; two describe the real logic behind why it happened this way.

citations.quote: For the Son of God became man so that we might become God.

questions.explanation: True. This level answered why God became man; the next level -- grace and the sacraments -- answers how that once-for-all saving work actually reaches each believer, in every generation since.

questions.prompt: The Catechism defines grace as:
choices: God's free and undeserved help to respond to his call
A reward earned through good works
A feeling of religious emotion
The natural human capacity for virtue
questions.correctAnswer: God's free and undeserved help to respond to his call
questions.explanation: Grace is never earned -- it is a free gift of God's own life, given so that we can respond to his call and share in his divine life.
questions.hint: This help is a gift, not something you earn.

citations.quote: Grace is favor, the free and undeserved help that God gives us to respond to his call to become children of God

questions.prompt: True or False: The Catholic Church recognizes seven sacraments, all instituted by Christ.
questions.explanation: The Church teaches that Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Reconciliation, Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders, and Matrimony were all instituted by Christ himself.
questions.hint: Count them: this number appears throughout the Catechism's sacramental teaching.

citations.quote: There are seven sacraments in the Church: Baptism, Confirmation or Chrismation, Eucharist, Penance, Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders, and Matrimony.

questions.prompt: Which three sacraments imprint a permanent, indelible spiritual mark on the soul that can never be repeated?
choices: Baptism, Confirmation, and Holy Orders
Baptism, Eucharist, and Reconciliation
Confirmation, Anointing of the Sick, and Matrimony
Eucharist, Reconciliation, and Matrimony
questions.explanation: These three sacraments each confer a 'character' -- a permanent spiritual seal -- which is why none of the three can ever be received a second time.
questions.hint: You can only receive each of these three sacraments once in your life.

citations.quote: The three sacraments of Baptism, Confirmation, and Holy Orders confer... a sacramental character or 'seal'... indelible, it remains forever... Therefore these sacraments can never be repeated.

questions.prompt: Grace that makes us holy and pleasing to God, dwelling in the soul as a lasting share in God's own life, is called ____ grace.
questions.explanation: Sanctifying grace is not a passing feeling but a stable disposition given by God, perfecting the soul so that it can live and act out of love for him.
questions.hint: This kind of grace is a lasting share in God's own life, not a passing feeling.

citations.quote: Sanctifying grace is an habitual gift, a stable and supernatural disposition that perfects the soul itself to enable it to live with God, to act by his love.

questions.prompt: Match each sacrament to the fact that describes it.

pairs.right: First sacrament of Christian initiation
Source and summit of the Christian life
Sacrament at the service of communion, uniting husband and wife
Sacrament of healing for the seriously ill

questions.explanation: The seven sacraments group naturally into initiation, healing, and service of communion -- each marking a stage or need in the Christian life.
questions.hint: One of these is called the 'source and summit' of the whole Christian life.

citations.quote: There are seven sacraments in the Church: Baptism, Confirmation or Chrismation, Eucharist, Penance, Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders, and Matrimony.
The Eucharist is 'the source and summit of the Christian life.'

questions.prompt: True or False: A sacrament's power to give grace depends on the personal holiness of the priest who administers it.
questions.explanation: The Church teaches the sacraments work 'ex opere operato' -- by the very fact of the action being performed -- so their power comes from Christ acting through the rite, not from the minister's personal sanctity.
questions.hint: The sacrament works even through an imperfect minister -- that's the whole point of this principle.

citations.quote: the sacraments act ex opere operato (literally: by the very fact of the action's being performed), i.e., by virtue of the saving work of Christ, accomplished once for all.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes actual grace from sanctifying grace?
choices: Sanctifying grace is a habitual, abiding gift; actual graces are God's interventions at particular moments
Sanctifying grace is for the clergy; actual grace is for the laity
Sanctifying grace is earned; actual grace is free
They are two names for the same reality
questions.correctAnswer: Sanctifying grace is a habitual, abiding gift; actual graces are God's interventions at particular moments
questions.explanation: One is a state, the other is an act. Sanctifying grace is a stable participation in God's own life; actual graces are the particular promptings that begin conversion or carry a person through a given moment.
questions.hint: One answers 'what am I?' and the other answers 'what is God doing right now?'

questions.prompt: True or False: The Church teaches that God has bound himself to the sacraments, so that grace can never reach anyone who, through no fault of their own, has not received them.
questions.explanation: False, and the distinction is deliberate. The Church is bound to the sacraments as the ordinary means Christ entrusted to her; God is not bound by them. That is why the Church can affirm the necessity of baptism and still hope for those who never received it.
questions.hint: The sentence is true of the Church but not of God — notice which one the question names.

questions.prompt: The Second Vatican Council calls the Eucharist the source and ____ of the Christian life.
questions.explanation: Source and summit together, not one or the other: everything in the Church flows from the Eucharist and everything is ordered back toward it. Calling it merely one sacrament among seven misses the claim being made.
questions.hint: The pair names both where the Christian life begins and where it is heading.

questions.prompt: Match each term about grace and the sacraments to its precise meaning.

pairs.right: Efficacy from the rite itself, not the minister's holiness
An indelible seal, conferred once and never repeated
A habitual share in God's own life
God's particular help at a given moment

questions.explanation: Two of these describe where sacramental power comes from and what it permanently marks; two describe what grace is in the soul. Keeping the pairs apart prevents the common error of treating grace as a quantity dispensed by a rite.
questions.hint: Two are about the sacrament, two are about the soul.

questions.prompt: Match each way the Church recognises baptism to what it means.

pairs.right: The sacrament itself, the ordinary means Christ entrusted to the Church
Death for the faith before receiving the sacrament
A catechumen's explicit desire, with repentance and charity
Seeking truth and doing God's will while ignorant of the Gospel

questions.explanation: All four are the Church's own teaching, and holding them together is what lets her say baptism is necessary without claiming that only the water-baptised are saved. The Church is bound to the sacraments; God is not bound by them.
questions.hint: One is the sacrament; the other three are how God acts where the sacrament was not received.

questions.prompt: True or False: Baptism of desire and baptism of blood are modern concessions, introduced to soften an older and harsher teaching.
questions.explanation: False. Both are long-standing in the Church's tradition, not recent adjustments. The martyr who dies unbaptised and the catechumen who dies before Easter were discussed by the Fathers, and the Catechism states both plainly. Presenting them as modern softening concedes a history that did not happen.
questions.hint: Ask whether the early Church had martyrs who died before they could be baptised.

questions.prompt: The Church teaches the sacraments act 'ex opere operato.' What does this precise phrase actually mean?
choices: By the sacramental action itself, by virtue of Christ's own saving work, not the minister's holiness
By the minister's own personal holiness, without which the sacrament simply fails to work
By the recipient's own emotional feeling of being close to God during the rite
By the size or wealth of the parish where the sacrament is celebrated
questions.correctAnswer: By the sacramental action itself, by virtue of Christ's own saving work, not the minister's holiness
questions.explanation: Ex opere operato -- literally, 'by the very fact of the action's being performed' -- means a validly celebrated sacrament's power comes from Christ's own once-for-all saving work, not from the minister's own personal worthiness.
questions.hint: Recall the previous level's own real teaching on whether a sacrament's power depends on the minister's own personal holiness.

citations.quote: the sacraments act ex opere operato (literally: by the very fact of the action's being performed), i.e., by virtue of the saving work of Christ, accomplished once for all.

questions.prompt: True or False: This precise teaching means a sacrament's real validity does not depend on whether the minister celebrating it happens to be in a state of grace.
questions.explanation: True, and this real precision matters enormously in practice -- a Catholic can trust a sacrament's own real validity without needing to investigate a minister's own private moral state, since its power comes from Christ, not from him.
questions.hint: Consider what a Catholic would need to know before trusting any sacrament, if this teaching were false.

citations.quote: the sacraments act ex opere operato (literally: by the very fact of the action's being performed), i.e., by virtue of the saving work of Christ, accomplished once for all.

questions.prompt: Why does this precise distinction actually matter for a believer's real, lived faith?
choices: Grace reaches a believer through Christ's own work, not a fallible human chain that could break
Because it means the sacraments have no real spiritual effect at all
Because it means any person, ordained or not, can validly celebrate any sacrament
Because it means a believer's own personal holiness plays no real role in receiving grace fruitfully
questions.correctAnswer: Grace reaches a believer through Christ's own work, not a fallible human chain that could break
questions.explanation: Without this precision, a believer's own real confidence in the sacraments would rest on an unverifiable chain of human worthiness. Ex opere operato anchors that confidence in Christ's own unchanging saving work instead.
questions.hint: Consider what would happen to a believer's own real trust in the sacraments without this precise teaching.

citations.quote: the sacraments act ex opere operato (literally: by the very fact of the action's being performed), i.e., by virtue of the saving work of Christ, accomplished once for all.

questions.prompt: True or False: Since a sacrament's validity does not depend on the minister's own personal holiness, a recipient's own disposition also makes no real difference to how fruitfully grace is received.
questions.explanation: False, and this is a real, careful second distinction -- validity (whether the sacrament truly happened) is one question; fruitfulness (how much grace a recipient actually receives) is another, and a recipient's own real disposition genuinely affects the second, even though it cannot affect the first.
questions.hint: Consider whether 'valid' and 'fruitfully received' are actually the exact same question.

citations.quote: the sacraments act ex opere operato (literally: by the very fact of the action's being performed), i.e., by virtue of the saving work of Christ, accomplished once for all.

questions.prompt: A theological student, working through this precise distinction for the first time, worries: 'Doesn't ex opere operato make the sacraments purely mechanical, as if grace worked like a vending machine?' What is the real, careful answer?
choices: No -- the sacraments still need real faith to bear fruit; this only secures validity against a fallible minister
Yes -- the recipient's own faith or disposition plays no real role in the sacraments whatsoever
No -- because sacraments actually depend entirely on the minister's own personal holiness after all
Yes -- but this is presented as a real advantage, since it makes personal faith entirely unnecessary
questions.correctAnswer: No -- the sacraments still need real faith to bear fruit; this only secures validity against a fallible minister
questions.explanation: This is exactly the real worry this precise vocabulary exists to answer carefully -- ex opere operato secures validity against a fallible human chain, without ever claiming a recipient's own real faith and disposition are irrelevant to how fruitfully grace is actually received.
questions.hint: Recall this level's own earlier real distinction between validity and fruitfulness.

citations.quote: the sacraments act ex opere operato (literally: by the very fact of the action's being performed), i.e., by virtue of the saving work of Christ, accomplished once for all.
